summary: Introduces the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) architecture and its terminology. It also lists architectural, modeling and protocol requirements for logically separating the control and data forwarding planes of an IP networking device. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A router is both a brain that decides and hands that move things. This describes splitting the two so they can be built and improved separately, and sets the goals for doing it.

questions: separation of control and forwarding planes
subtitle: The terminology and requirements for splitting a router's brain from its packet-moving hardware.

tldr.problem: Routers and similar devices bundle control functions such as routing protocols and per-packet forwarding into one integrated box, so the two cannot evolve or be built independently.
tldr.mechanism: The ForCES architecture splits a network element into Control Elements and Forwarding Elements that talk over a standard protocol. The RFC defines the terms and lists architectural, forwarding element model and protocol requirements.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document and does not define the protocol itself. It sets the goals that a ForCES protocol and a model of forwarding elements must meet.

facts.label: Scale target
facts.value: Hundreds of FEs, tens of thousands of ports

facts.label: Roles
facts.value: CEs are masters, FEs are slaves

today: RFC 3654 is an Informational requirements document and the data does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It sets goals for ForCES but does not itself define the protocol or the FE model.

sections.title: Control Plane and Forwarding Plane
sections.content:
An IP network element is made of logically separate parts that cooperate yet look like one integrated device from outside. Two kinds of components exist. Forwarding-plane components are typically ASIC, network-processor or general-purpose processor based devices that handle the data path. Control-plane components are typically general-purpose processors that run routing or signaling protocols (the RFC names RIP, OSPF and RSVP).

In a router, the control plane steers forwarding by manipulating forwarding tables, per-flow QoS tables and access control lists. Today these are combined into a single functional whole. A standard set of mechanisms for connecting them would give more scalability and let each plane evolve independently, which promotes faster innovation.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has a thinking part that makes decisions and a doing part that moves packets. If they were separate pieces with a standard way to talk, each could get better on its own.

sections.title: ForCES Terminology
sections.content:
A Forwarding Element (FE) is a logical entity that does per-packet processing as directed by a Control Element. A Control Element (CE) runs control and signaling protocols and instructs one or more FEs how to process packets. A Network Element (NE) is one or more CEs plus one or more FEs, and looks like a single point of management to the outside.

The physical hardware is described by Physical Forwarding Elements and Physical Control Elements. An FE may be a single blade, part of a PFE or several PFEs.

The ForCES protocol means only the post-association phase protocol between CEs and FEs, a master-slave protocol where FEs are slaves and CEs are masters. FE Managers and CE Managers work in the earlier pre-association phase to decide which FEs and CEs belong together. That phase and its protocols are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss pieces are control elements and the worker pieces are forwarding elements. Together they pretend to be one big machine.

sections.title: The Architectural Requirements
sections.content:
The chief components of an NE are the CE, the FE and the interconnect protocol. The CE might control an FE by changing its forwarding tables, the state of its interfaces, or a NAT binding. Section 4 of the RFC lists fourteen architectural requirements. Some highlights:

  • CEs and FEs MUST connect over a variety of interconnects, with Ethernet, bus backplanes and ATM fabrics given as examples.
  • A packet MUST be able to enter the NE through one FE and leave through another.
  • The NE MUST appear as a single functional device. In a router the TTL is decremented only once however many FEs the packet passes.
  • The architecture MUST scale to at least hundreds of FEs and tens of thousands of ports, and FEs and CEs MUST be able to join and leave dynamically.
  • It MUST support CE redundancy or failover, including presetting what an FE does if it loses its CE.
  • FEs MUST redirect control packets such as RIP and OSPF messages to the CE, and any proposed architecture MUST explain how it supports the router functions of RFC 1812.
sections.plainLanguage: Many worker pieces plus a boss should still act like one machine, keep going if the boss fails, and let pieces be added or removed while running.

sections.title: The Forwarding Element Model
sections.content:
For a CE to control an FE it must understand how that FE processes packets. The RFC therefore requires an FE model that expresses an FE's logical packet processing, with both a capability model and a state model of the current configuration. The model MUST allow variations of logical functions, describe their order (for example whether other functions see pre-NAT or post-NAT addresses), and allow several instances of the same function in one path. It SHOULD be easy to extend.

A minimal set of logical functions that the model MUST be able to express includes port functions, IPv4 and IPv6 unicast and multicast forwarding, QoS functions (metering, policing, shaping, queuing), generic filtering, encapsulation and tunneling, and encryption types. The model must also describe off-loaded functions that run asynchronously, such as OSPF Hello processing. The minimal set does not oblige every FE to provide all of this.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss needs a menu that lists what each worker can do and in what order. That menu has to be flexible enough for workers with different skills.

sections.title: ForCES Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
Section 6 lists fifteen requirements for the protocol between CEs and FEs. The protocol MUST let CEs discover FE capabilities using the FE model, add and remove entries, set parameters, query statistics and receive events. It MUST also support:

  • Redirect and mirror: redirection ends processing at the FE, while mirroring sends a copy to the CE and lets the original continue.
  • Command bundling: an ordered group of commands sent in as few messages as possible, with optional all-or-nothing semantics.
  • Reliability that varies by payload: configuration such as ACLs and FIB entries must be delivered robustly, while redirected packets and heartbeats need not be strictly reliable.
  • Multihop: when CEs and FEs are more than one L3 hop apart, use an existing RFC 2914 compliant L4 protocol such as TCP or SCTP.
  • Message priority, topology exchange, dynamic association, asynchronous event notification, and mechanisms to protect against denial of service by installing filters and rate limiters.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages between boss and workers must handle urgent and unimportant notes differently, bundle orders together, and survive rough conditions.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section only points to architecture requirement 5 and protocol requirement 2. The architecture must prevent unauthorized elements from joining an NE. For the protocol, it MUST be possible to ensure the integrity of all messages and protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, and to make all messages private. The architecture MUST select a means of authentication for CEs and FEs.

When CEs and FEs are inside one box on a backplane, the architecture MAY rely on the box's physical security, and protocol mechanisms may be turned off. When they are connected over a network, security mechanisms MUST be specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted workers may join, and the messages must not be changed or read by outsiders. Inside one locked box, the locks on the box can do some of that job.
